Q: How to split the Git Bash into more than one “view” in Windows? A:

Git Bash, won't allow users to split the screen in to two as the features don't exist. The only way is to use alternative or use ConEmu to configure, my personal preference would be Cmder (console emulator) and other options would be Moba Xterm. Cmder is open source and completely free. This would be much easier than configuring ConEmu.

  • Cmder: https://cmder.app/
  • MobaXterm: https://mobaxterm.mobatek.net/

Q: Creating an android sync tool A:

"Those details are still being worked out" means you still need find out what does "sync" mean in your context. What does your app do with the files?

If your app/device is a jukebox using regular media like audio/video files then an MTP service may be sufficient. If you need something more specialized then you may need to consider using a USB serial library and setup a connection on both ends to communicate. Another thing to look at is Android Open Accessory Protocol. Both will require an Android app and a PC side app to communicate with Android and transmit data. Only you can investigate what option is appropriate for your problem/hardware.

Q: Formatting lsof output into parsable structure A:

Here is how you can do it with Powershell.

lsof -F? will print all possible fields:

lsof:   ID    field description
         a    access: r = read; w = write; u = read/write
         c    command name
         d    device character code
         D    major/minor device number as 0x<hex>
         f    file descriptor
         G    file flaGs
         i    inode number
         k    link count
         K    task ID (TID)
         l    lock: r/R = read; w/W = write; u = read/write
         L    login name
         m    marker between repeated output
         M    task comMand name
         n    comment, name, Internet addresses
         o    file offset as 0t<dec> or 0x<hex>
         p    process ID (PID)
         g    process group ID (PGID)
         P    protocol name
         r    raw device number as 0x<hex>
         R    paRent PID
         s    file size
         S    stream module and device names
         t    file type
         T    TCP/TPI info
         u    user ID (UID)
         0    (zero) use NUL field terminator instead of NL

# We will query for same fields as Robert Phillips did in his answer:
$out = lsof -F pcuftDsin

# Got 822634 lines

# First, let's verify the structure. 
# From those lines we will keep only first char.
$outLine = $out | % {$_.Substring(0,1)} | Join-String
# > pcuftnftnftnfnpcuftnftnftnfnpcuftnftnftnfnpcuftnf...

# Make sure P is always followed by C, C by U, U by F.
'p[^c]','c[^u]','u[^f]' | % {$outLine -match $_}
# > False,False,False

Now we know p field means lsof started describing new process, each process can have multiple files and each file starts with f field.

# Now, create objects from original lsof output
$objs = @(); $obj = $null
foreach ($str in $out) {
$char = $str.Substring(0,1)

if ($char -eq 'p') { 
  # New process
  if ($obj) { $objs += [pscustomobject]$obj; } # Don't add initial null
  $obj = [ordered]@{} 
}

if (($char -eq 'f') -and ($obj[$char])) {
  # New file for same process. Create new obj with same pcu
  $objNew = [ordered]@{ p=$obj.p; c=$obj.c; u=$obj.u }

  $objs += [pscustomobject]$obj
  $obj = $objNew
}

# Add property to current object
$obj[$char] = $str.Substring(1)
}
# Add last object
$objs += [pscustomobject]$obj

We got $objs array of ~150000 files:

> $objs | Get-Random

p : 2548
c : variety
u : 1000
f : mem
t : REG
D : 0x10305
s : 2320
i : 1189461
n : /var/cache/fontconfig/49f0de54bdd920fe4f0dfd4cbac43e6b-le64.cache-9

Here is how we can build new array with readable property names:

# First, create a char->readable label mapping
@'
p: PID
c: Command
u: User
f: FD
t: Type
D: Device
s: SizeOff
i: Node
n: Name
'@ -split '\n' | ForEach-Object {$heaMap = [ordered]@{}}{ 
  $arr = $_  -split ': '
  $heaMap[$arr[0]] = $arr[1]
}

# Now for each object iterate though it's props and create a new obj
$objsNew = $objs | ForEach-Object {
  $renamed = [ordered]@{}
  $_.PSObject.properties | ForEach-Object {$label = $heaMap[$_.name]; $renamed[$label] = $_.value}
  [pscustomobject]$renamed
}

Now, we can convert new objects to json:

> $objsNew | Get-Random -Count 2 | ConvertTo-Json

Q: How to pre-read I2c message length/header - Python A:

Bottom line: use an existing Python I2C library, e.g. smbus2, and check your device's documentation on how exactly to read a chunk of data longer than the 32 bytes that a single I2C read operation allows.

The issue is that the I2C mailbox is cleared as soon as it is read so I cannot simply implement my read code twice - once for the header and again for the full message and payload.

This sounds fishy. If that's how you describe it is, the device either deletes its data before it's read -- which is hardly the case -- or it has some way to determine what data you have already processed and what you didn't -- which is also impossible because all it does is send the data onto the wire, with no way of knowing what happens to it next.

According to smbus2.SMBus.read_block_data documentation, the I2C protocol only allows to read up to 32 bytes from a device register at a time. So there must be some procedure in place in the device allowing you to read more without the device discarding what you are about to read.

My guess is that you probably read the first (up to) 32 bytes, extract the length field, then you know how many more reads you need to perform. Maybe you also need to set some other "lock" flag in the device to signal it that you're in the process of reading the multi-chunk data.

Q: The pointer existential crisis dilemma: If pointer stores memory address then how are memory addresses of a pointers stored? A:

Pointers are objects as any other objects of other types. You may take an address of any object that is not a temporary object or is not declared with storage class specifier register.

Consider the following declaration

T x;

where T is a type.

When you can declare a pointer that points to this variable

T *p = &x;

Now you can define the type T as for example

typedef int T;

In this case the type of the pointer p will be T *. That is for the variable p the program allocates memory of the size sizeof( p ) that i the same as sizeof( int * ) and stores there the value of the address of the variable x.

The type T can be defined in turn as a pointer type as for example

typedef int ***T;

In this case the variable x itself will have the pointer type int *** and the variable p will have a pointer to pointer type that is int ****. The memory for pointers are allocated the same way as for other scalar types.

Q: Passing SQL query in url A:

provide a restful style interact with you sql database.
